lessons.title: Rooming, turnover, and the discharge you own
lessons.body:
Three moments of a visit belong almost entirely to the tech: getting the patient into the room, getting them out the door, and getting the room ready for the next one. Each has a sequence, and the sequence is what keeps a department moving.

## Rooming, in order

1. **Two identifiers,** name and date of birth, matched against the armband and the label. Every time, including the patient you just wheeled from triage.
2. **Undress and gown.** You cannot assess what you cannot see. Chest pain, abdominal pain, trauma, syncope, weakness, fever without a source, any possible rash, and any diabetic foot complaint all come out of their clothes. Keep them covered while you do it, and offer a warm blanket immediately after.
3. **Belongings.** Inventory them, label the bag, and route valuables per policy. Dentures, hearing aids, glasses and prosthetics go in labeled containers, never in a towel or on a meal tray, because that is exactly how they end up in the linen chute.
4. **Attach what is needed.** Monitor leads, pulse oximeter, and a blood pressure cuff whose bladder wraps about `80%` of the arm — a cuff that is too small reads falsely high.
5. **Full set of vitals** including a temperature and a pain score, plus a glucose on anyone altered, diabetic, or weak.
6. **Set the room.** Bed low, rails per policy, call bell in reach, emesis bag and tissues within reach, urinal or bedpan if mobility is limited, curtain closed.
7. **Say what happens next** and roughly when you will be back.

> **Key:** Anticipate the workup while you room. Chest pain gets the monitor and an EKG. Abdominal pain in anyone of childbearing potential gets a urine cup on the way to the bathroom, because the pregnancy test gates the imaging. Possible sepsis gets culture bottles at the bedside.

## The discharge you own

The provider decides, the nurse instructs and gives prescriptions, and then most of the last fifteen minutes is yours: removing leads and cleaning adhesive off the skin, returning belongings against the written inventory, bringing the wheelchair, and walking them out.

Use that walk. A patient who cannot stand without holding the wall, who is still saturating `89%`, who is still visibly intoxicated, who has no coat in January, or who has no ride at `0300` is a patient the department is about to lose track of. Say it before they leave, to the nurse, in plain words: "Before she goes, her last walking saturation was 89 and she needed two people to stand."

> **On shift:** Two questions at the door catch most failed discharges: do you have a way to get home, and do you know what would make you come back?

## Turnover under pressure

A quick turn takes `5 to 10 minutes` and a terminal clean `20 to 30`. Your part of the quick turn is fixed: strip the linens into the hamper, wipe the stretcher rails, mattress, handles, cables, cuff and monitor screen with the approved disinfectant, replace the sheet and pillowcase, restock gowns, pads, gloves, electrodes, emesis bags and blood tubes, hang the cuff and probe back up, lower the bed, and put the call bell in reach.

Then do the step everyone forgets: **mark the bed clean and available in the tracking system.** A perfectly cleaned room that the board still shows as dirty is a bed the department does not have.

> **Trap:** Disinfectant wipes only work if the surface stays visibly wet for the full contact time on the label, often `1 to 4 minutes`. Wiping something dry in fifteen seconds is theater. Rooms with contact precautions, especially C. difficile, need the specific agent and the full clean by environmental services — that one is not yours to shortcut.
keyPoints: Room in a fixed order: two identifiers, gown, belongings inventory, monitor and cuff, full vitals, room setup, expectations.
Undress every patient whose complaint could hide on the skin or the trunk, and cover them immediately afterward.
Use the walk to the door as a last screen: unsteady gait, low saturation, no ride, no coat, still intoxicated.
A quick turn is 5 to 10 minutes and ends with marking the bed available in the tracking system.
Disinfectants require the labeled wet contact time, usually 1 to 4 minutes, and precaution rooms need the full environmental services clean.

checks.q: You are rooming a 28-year-old with lower abdominal pain. Which anticipatory step saves the most time?
choices: Setting up a suture tray
Collecting a urine specimen on the way past the bathroom, since a pregnancy test gates imaging decisions
Placing her on continuous cardiac monitoring
Obtaining a 12-lead EKG
checks.why: In anyone of childbearing potential, the pregnancy result shapes both the differential and whether CT is used. A urine specimen obtained at rooming can save an hour of waiting later.

checks.q: You finish cleaning and restocking a room in six minutes but do not update the tracking system. What is the consequence?
choices: None, since the room is physically ready
The board still shows the bed as unavailable, so the department cannot place a waiting patient in it
Environmental services will be charged for the clean
The next patient's chart will not open
checks.why: Flow runs on the board, not on reality. A clean room the system believes is dirty is invisible to the charge nurse assigning beds, and the waiting room keeps growing.

checks.q: Why does a blood pressure cuff that is too small matter?
choices: It reads falsely low and hides hypertension
It is uncomfortable but accurate
It reads falsely high, which can trigger unnecessary workup or mask a falling pressure trend
It only affects automatic machines, not manual readings
checks.why: An undersized bladder requires more pressure to occlude the artery, so the reading comes out high. The bladder should encircle roughly 80 percent of the arm.

lessons.title: Taking an EMS handoff
lessons.body:
For sixty seconds, the crew standing at the foot of the stretcher is the only source in the world for information that nobody will ever be able to reconstruct. How you behave in that minute decides how much of it survives.

## Stop moving

Unless the patient is actively dying, the transfer happens **after** the report, not during it. Nothing destroys a handoff faster than three people counting to three while the paramedic is still talking. Stand still, face the crew, and let them give it in their order.

Then do the transfer deliberately: agree on a count, keep oxygen and the monitor running through the move, and switch monitors last. Note the time the patient came onto your monitor.

## What the report contains

Most crews use a version of the same skeleton:

- **Mechanism or complaint,** and the time it started.
- **Injuries or findings** on their exam.
- **Signs:** vital signs with times, including the **first** set, which nobody else will ever see.
- **Treatment** given, the time, and the response.

> **Key:** The first prehospital blood pressure is a number that exists in one place. If the patient arrives at `104/60` after fluids, only the crew knows they were `72/40` in the driveway. Write it down before you forget it.

## What the tech should personally capture

These are the items that get lost in the shuffle and that you can be the person who preserves.

1. **Times.** Onset, and for any neurologic complaint, the **last known well** time plus the name and phone number of the person who witnessed it.
2. **The prehospital 12-lead,** and whether an alert was called from the field. Put the tracing in a provider's hand, not on a counter.
3. **Medications given en route** with times: aspirin, nitroglycerin, naloxone, epinephrine, albuterol, glucose.
4. **The patient's own medication bottles or list,** which families hand to crews and crews hand to nobody.
5. **The scene.** How the patient was found and in what position, how much blood was there, pill bottles present, a note, whether the home had heat and food, who else was there, whether a helmet or seatbelt was used. This is information that only existed for four minutes and only three people saw it.
6. **Contact information** for the family member who is not riding along.
7. **Belongings,** counted against what the crew says they brought.

## The tech's three questions

When the report is thin, these fill most of the gap: what was the first blood pressure, what time did this start or when were they last normal, and did they get anything from you?

## Afterward

Repeat what you captured to the nurse immediately, rather than being the only person holding it. For chest pain, obtain your own `12-lead` on arrival even if EMS did one, and get it to the provider inside `10 minutes` of arrival — the clock is your department's, not the ambulance's.

> **On shift:** Give the crew their equipment back, restock what you used, and sign what needs signing. Crews remember which departments make them wait forty minutes for a stretcher sheet, and they are the same people who will call ahead for you on the bad one.
keyPoints: Complete the verbal report before moving the patient, then transfer on a count with oxygen and monitoring continuous.
The first prehospital blood pressure and the time of onset exist only with the crew; write them down immediately.
For any neurologic complaint, capture last known well plus the witness's name and phone number.
Preserve the scene details nobody else saw: position found, blood loss, pill bottles, notes, home conditions, restraint use.
Repeat an EKG on arrival for chest pain and get it to a provider within 10 minutes of arrival regardless of the prehospital tracing.

checks.q: EMS arrives with a hypotensive patient. Your charge nurse wants the patient moved quickly. What is the correct handling of the verbal report?
choices: Move the patient during the report to save time
Complete the verbal report first unless the patient is actively dying, then transfer on a count with monitoring continuous
Skip the report and read the run sheet later
Have the crew give the report only to the physician
checks.why: Information given during a transfer is lost. Unless the patient requires immediate intervention, the report comes first, and then the move happens deliberately.

checks.q: A patient with slurred speech arrives by EMS. Which single piece of information most changes the patient's treatment options?
choices: The prehospital pulse oximetry reading
The patient's insurance status
The last known well time, with the witness's contact information
The name of the transporting agency
checks.why: Thrombolytic and thrombectomy eligibility runs on the clock from when the patient was last normal. If the witness leaves without giving a phone number, that window may become unverifiable.

lessons.title: What is in the room and on the carts
lessons.body:
Speed in an emergency department is mostly knowing where things are. This is the inventory, learned once, that stops you from opening four drawers while somebody bleeds.

## A standard room

Stretcher with rails and a brake. Wall **suction** with a canister, tubing and a rigid tip. Wall **oxygen** with a flowmeter, nasal cannula, nonrebreather and a bag-valve mask. Monitor with a five-lead cable, pulse oximeter probe, end-tidal carbon dioxide line, and blood pressure cuffs in at least three sizes. Sharps container, glove boxes, gowns, linens, absorbent pads, emesis bags, urinal and bedpan, tissues, wall otoscope and ophthalmoscope, biohazard bin, computer, call bell.

## The blood draw tray

Tourniquets, alcohol and chlorhexidine, gauze, tape, butterfly sets, straight needles, the vacutainer hub, blood culture bottles, and the tubes. Learn the **order of draw**, because it prevents additives from contaminating the next tube: blood cultures first, then light blue (citrate), then gold or red (serum), then green (heparin), then lavender (EDTA), then gray (fluoride). Labels go on at the bedside, never at the desk.

## The crash cart

Layouts vary, but the logic does not. On top: the monitor-defibrillator, pads, gel and a backboard.

| Drawer | Contents |
|---|---|
| Airway | Laryngoscope handle and blades, endotracheal tubes, stylet, syringe, bougie, supraglottic airways, oral and nasal airways, carbon dioxide detector |
| Circulation | IV catheters, intraosseous drill and needles, fluids, tubing, pressure bag |
| Medications | Epinephrine `0.1 mg/mL` prefilled syringes, amiodarone, calcium, sodium bicarbonate, atropine, adenosine, dextrose, naloxone |
| Procedures | Central line kits, chest tube tray, suture, scalpel |

The cart is sealed with a numbered breakaway tag and carries a **checklist someone signs every shift**. In many departments that someone is the tech. You confirm the tag is intact and the number matches the log, the defibrillator passed its self-test and the battery is charged, the suction works, the portable oxygen cylinder reads above about `1,500 psi`, and nothing on the outside has expired.

> **Key:** Three failures stop a resuscitation before it starts: no suction, a dead defibrillator battery, and an empty oxygen tank. Check all three at the start of every shift, in every resus bay. It takes ninety seconds.

## The other carts

Difficult airway cart with video laryngoscopy. Procedure carts for central lines, chest tubes, lumbar puncture, pelvic and precipitous delivery, laceration repair, splinting, and burns. An eye tray with fluorescein strips, a slit lamp or Wood's lamp, and an irrigation lens. The pediatric cart with a length-based tape and color-coded equipment. A warming cabinet for blankets and fluids. Isolation carts stocked with gowns, face shields and N95 respirators.

## Where things travel

Specimens go to the pneumatic tube system or a runner. Learn two local rules before your first send: which specimens are never tubed, and that nothing leaves the bedside without a label. An unlabeled specimen is a discarded specimen and a repeat needle stick for the patient.

> **On shift:** Restock what you use, in the moment. The cost of replacing one `18-gauge` catheter is thirty seconds now, or four minutes at `0300` when somebody else needs it and the drawer is empty.
keyPoints: Know the standard room cold: suction, oxygen, monitor, cuffs in three sizes, and the consumables.
Order of draw is blood cultures, light blue, gold or red, green, lavender, gray, and labels go on at the bedside.
The crash cart is airway, circulation, medications and procedures, sealed with a numbered tag and a per-shift checklist.
Check suction, defibrillator battery and oxygen cylinder pressure in every resus bay at the start of every shift.
An unlabeled specimen is discarded, which means a repeat stick for the patient.

checks.q: Which set of checks matters most when verifying a resuscitation bay at the start of your shift?
choices: Linen count, glove sizes and pillow supply
Computer login, chair position and lighting
Suction working, defibrillator self-test passed with a charged battery, oxygen cylinder above about 1,500 psi, crash cart tag intact
Wall art, curtain condition and floor cleanliness
checks.why: Those four failures stop a resuscitation before it begins. Everything else can be improvised; none of these can.

checks.q: In what order should blood tubes be filled?
choices: Lavender, gold, light blue, cultures, gray
Blood cultures, light blue, gold or red, green, lavender, gray
Gray, green, gold, lavender, cultures
Any order, as long as each tube is filled to the line
checks.why: The sequence prevents additive carryover from invalidating results, and cultures come first to minimize contamination. Filling out of order produces falsely abnormal potassium and clotting values.

lessons.title: Four checklists: stroke, trauma, code, sedation
lessons.body:
In an alert, nobody has the bandwidth to tell you what to do. These four lists are what a tech owns, and knowing them by heart is what makes you useful in the first two minutes.

## Stroke alert

1. **Last known well time** and the witness's phone number. Everything downstream depends on it.
2. **Glucose immediately.** Hypoglycemia imitates a stroke perfectly and is fixable in ninety seconds.
3. **A real weight in kilograms,** from a bed scale, not a guess. Thrombolytic dosing is weight-based, and an estimate is not acceptable.
4. Full vitals, a `12-lead`, monitor, pulse oximetry, and blood pressures per policy.
5. IV access and labs if you are credentialed, drawn without delaying anything.
6. Nothing by mouth, including pills and sips of water.
7. **Do not delay the CT scanner for any of the above.** Targets are roughly `25 minutes` door-to-CT and `60 minutes` door-to-needle. Labs and lines can travel with the patient.

## Trauma alert

1. **Protect yourself:** gown, gloves, mask with eye shield, and a lead apron if imaging is coming into the room.
2. **Prepare the room:** warm it, warm the fluids, monitor on, suction and oxygen tested, shears out, rapid infuser and chest tube tray available, slide board ready.
3. **Expose completely.** Cut clothing along the seams. For an assault or shooting, place clothing in **paper** bags, not plastic, and do not cut through holes in the fabric.
4. Roll on the team leader's command for the back exam, then get blankets back on. Hypothermia worsens bleeding in trauma patients, and the room is cold for the staff, not the patient.
5. First full set of vitals, monitor, and blood tubes including a type and screen, labeled at the bedside.

## Cardiac arrest

1. **Compressions first,** `100 to 120` per minute, at least `2 inches` deep, full recoil, pauses under `10 seconds`, switching every `2 minutes`.
2. Pads on early. Know where the pads and the backboard live in every room.
3. Count out loud, watch the clock, and rotate before your quality drops rather than after.
4. Retrieve, run and restock: airway cart, ultrasound, specimens to the lab.
5. End-tidal carbon dioxide above `10 mmHg` suggests compressions are adequate; a sudden jump to `35 to 40` often means pulses have returned.
6. Afterward: restock the bay before anything else, then help with the body and the family, and attend the debrief.

## Procedural sedation

1. **Before anything is pushed:** monitor with continuous pulse oximetry and end-tidal carbon dioxide, oxygen on, **suction tested**, a bag-valve mask at the head of the bed, the airway cart in the room, and a person whose only job is recording vital signs.
2. Stay in the room. Sedation is one of the few situations where a tech leaving to answer a call bell is the wrong call.
3. Your eyes belong on the chest and the monitor. Call out snoring, apnea, or a falling saturation the instant it appears, out loud, without waiting to be sure.
4. Vitals at the interval policy sets, commonly every `5 minutes`, continuing through recovery.
5. Discharge from sedation requires baseline mental status, protected airway, stable vitals, and a responsible adult; no driving for `24 hours`.

> **Key:** In all four, the tech's highest-value actions are the same three: get the number nobody else can get, prepare the room before it is needed, and say what you see out loud.

> **Trap:** The most common tech error in an alert is doing a useful task at the wrong time — drawing labs while the stroke patient should already be rolling to CT, or hunting for a gown while compressions have not started.
keyPoints: Stroke: last known well, immediate glucose, a scale weight in kilograms, and nothing delays the CT scanner.
Trauma: personal protective equipment, a warm room, complete exposure with paper bags for evidence, and blankets back on immediately.
Code: compressions at 100 to 120 per minute and at least 2 inches, switching every 2 minutes, with pauses under 10 seconds.
End-tidal carbon dioxide above 10 mmHg suggests adequate compressions; a jump to 35 to 40 suggests return of circulation.
Sedation: suction tested and a bag-valve mask at the head before any drug, a dedicated recorder, and you do not leave the room.

checks.q: A stroke alert patient arrives and you have not yet drawn labs or placed an IV. The CT scanner is open now. What is correct?
choices: Go to CT now; labs and access can be obtained on the way or after the scan
Complete labs and two IVs first so the team has everything
Wait for the neurologist to arrive before moving
Obtain a full 12-lead and repeat vitals before moving
checks.why: Door-to-CT of about 25 minutes drives every treatment decision. Useful tasks done at the wrong moment are the classic tech error in a stroke alert.

checks.q: Why is a bed-scale weight in kilograms required during a stroke alert?
choices: For billing purposes
Because thrombolytic dosing is weight-based and an estimated weight can produce a dangerous dose
To determine which stretcher to use
It is not needed if the patient can state their weight
checks.why: Estimates by staff and by patients are routinely off by enough to matter for a weight-based clot-dissolving drug. Get a measured weight, in kilograms, early.

checks.q: During procedural sedation you notice the patient begin to snore and the saturation drift from 99 to 93 percent. What do you do?
choices: Wait to see whether it corrects itself
Silence the monitor alarm and recheck in a minute
Say it out loud immediately to the provider and nurse while repositioning the airway as directed
Leave to find the respiratory therapist
checks.why: Snoring is partial airway obstruction and a falling saturation during sedation is an early warning. Announcing it immediately is the entire reason you are standing there.

lessons.title: Consults, admissions, and how a patient actually leaves
lessons.body:
A disposition is a word on the board and an hour of machinery underneath it. Knowing the machinery tells you why patients wait, and where a tech can shorten it.

## The consult

The provider decides another specialty needs to weigh in, and the clerk pages or the provider calls directly. The consultant may be in the building or asleep at home; hospital policy usually sets an expectation such as a callback within `30 minutes` and arrival within `60`.

Common ED consults: cardiology for heart attacks and admissions to telemetry, general surgery for appendicitis and obstruction, orthopedics for fractures that need reduction, obstetrics, neurology for stroke, psychiatry or the crisis screener, urology, ear-nose-throat, ophthalmology, and poison control at `1-800-222-1222`.

Your contribution is preparation. A consultant arriving to find the patient gowned, the urine already collected, the EKG already on the chart and the family present is a consultant who makes a decision in ten minutes instead of forty. Tell the nurse the moment a consultant walks in.

## The admission sequence

Six steps, each of which is a place a patient waits:

1. The ED provider decides to admit.
2. They pick a **service**: hospitalist medicine, surgery, cardiology, pediatrics, intensive care.
3. They call the accepting provider, who may want to see the patient first.
4. Admission orders are written.
5. A **bed request** goes to patient flow, and a specific bed is assigned. The level matters: general medical-surgical, telemetry for cardiac monitoring, step-down, or ICU.
6. Nurse-to-nurse report, then transport upstairs.

**Observation** status is a middle path of roughly `24 hours` for patients who need serial testing rather than a full admission. To the patient it looks identical to an admission; it is a status and billing distinction, and it is not yours to explain.

## Boarding is a patient care assignment

When the upstairs is full, admitted patients stay in your beds for hours. Those patients quietly become nobody's priority, and that is where harm happens. A boarder still needs vitals on schedule, help to the bathroom, repositioning about every `2 hours` to protect the skin, a meal if the orders allow it, oral care, and the same rounding loop as anyone else.

> **Key:** The admitted patient in the hallway is the most likely person in the department to develop a pressure injury, fall, or deteriorate unnoticed. Round on boarders the way you round on new patients.

## Transfers out

When the hospital cannot provide the service — a burn center, a pediatric trauma center, a cath lab, an inpatient psychiatric bed — the patient transfers. EMTALA still governs it: stabilize within your capability, obtain an accepting physician and facility, document the risks and benefits, and send the record with the patient.

The tech assembles the packet: printed chart and orders, EKG tracings, imaging pushed or burned to a disc, belongings, and the transfer form. Anything you forget arrives by fax three hours later, if at all.

> **On shift:** Learn the practical map, not the floor plan: which elevator reaches the intensive care unit, where the cath lab is, which units take telemetry patients, where the operating room holding area is, and which hallway is shortest with a monitored patient and an oxygen tank.
keyPoints: A consult runs on preparation: patient gowned, specimens collected, tracings on the chart, family present, and the nurse told when the consultant arrives.
Admission has six waiting points: decision, service selection, accepting provider, orders, bed request and assignment, and nurse-to-nurse report.
Bed level is a monitoring decision: medical-surgical, telemetry, step-down, or intensive care.
Boarders need the full rounding loop, including repositioning about every 2 hours, because they are the patients most likely to be forgotten.
Transfers require an accepting physician and facility plus the complete record packet: chart, EKGs, imaging and belongings.

checks.q: An admitted patient has been boarding in a hallway bed for five hours. What does the tech owe them?
choices: Nothing further, since the inpatient team now owns the patient
The full rounding loop: scheduled vitals, toileting, repositioning roughly every 2 hours, meals per orders, and oral care
Only vital signs, once per shift
Only what the inpatient nurse requests by phone
checks.why: Until the patient physically leaves, the ED provides the care. Boarders are the patients most likely to develop pressure injuries, fall, or deteriorate without anyone noticing.

checks.q: A patient is being transferred to a burn center. Which item is the tech most responsible for assembling?
choices: The accepting physician's agreement
The risk and benefit discussion with the patient
The transfer packet: printed record, EKG tracings, imaging, belongings and the transfer form
The insurance authorization
checks.why: Physician-to-physician acceptance and the risk discussion belong to the provider. The record packet is the piece that predictably gets left behind, and it is a tech task.

lessons.title: Professionalism when it is hard
lessons.body:
Most professionalism advice is useless because it describes easy situations. These are the five that actually happen, with what to say.

## The colleague who is rude to you

Separate a bad moment from a pattern. A nurse who snaps at hour ten of a terrible shift is having a moment, and the correct response is to let it go and keep working.

A pattern is different. Address it once, privately, specifically, and without an audience: "When you said that in front of the patient's daughter, it made it hard for me to do my job. Can we handle it differently next time?" If it continues, it goes to the charge nurse and then the ED educator or manager. What it never does is get returned in kind, or litigated in a hallway where patients can hear.

## The provider who is short with you

Usually this is cognitive load, not contempt. Somebody tracking nine patients and one crashing does not have room for a paragraph. Adapt: lead with the ask, keep it to one sentence, and pick a moment when they are not mid-thought. "Room 4, do you want the EKG repeated?" gets an answer; a three-sentence preamble does not.

If it crosses into demeaning or public humiliation, that is a separate problem, and it goes to your supervisor rather than into your bloodstream.

## The mistake you made

You will mislabel a tube, miss a scheduled recheck, drop a specimen, or be in the room when a patient goes to the floor. The sequence is fixed and it is the same one clinicians at every level use:

1. Patient first. Assess, get vitals, get the nurse.
2. Tell the nurse what happened, in plain words, immediately.
3. Document objectively, with no conclusions and no blame, including who you notified and when.
4. File the incident or safety report, including for near-misses where nothing happened.
5. Ask what to change so it does not repeat.

> **Key:** Concealment is what turns an error into a catastrophe. The redraw, the repeat scan and the missed vital sign are all survivable. A chart that does not match reality is not.

## The patient who asks you out

Be warm, be clear, do not negotiate. "I'm here as your tech, and that's the only relationship I can have with a patient." Then tell your nurse, so it is documented and so you are not alone with it.

No personal phone numbers, no social media, no visiting off shift. Persistent sexual comments, exposure, or touching are not part of the job: step out of the room, get help, and report it. Your department has a process, and using it is the professional response, not an overreaction. Use a chaperone for sensitive exams every time, regardless of anyone's gender.

## The request to do something you should not

Someone senior, busy, and well-meaning will ask you to give a medication, take a verbal order, or chart something you did not do. Offer the part you can do and hand off the part you cannot: "I am not signed off on that, but I'll set it all up and grab the nurse." Charting something you did not personally do is falsification, and there is no version of it that is a favor.

> **On shift:** The privacy rules are absolute and they are audited. No photos, ever. No looking up your own chart, a family member's chart, or a coworker's chart. No discussing patients in elevators, hallways or the cafeteria. No posting anything about a shift, even with names removed, because de-identified stories are routinely identifiable to the people involved.
keyPoints: Separate a bad moment from a pattern; address a pattern once, privately and specifically, then escalate.
A short-tempered provider usually reflects cognitive load, so lead with the ask in one sentence at a workable moment.
After your own error: patient first, tell the nurse immediately, document objectively, file the report, ask what to change.
Decline romantic or sexual attention clearly and tell your nurse; persistent harassment gets reported, not absorbed.
Never chart what you did not do, and never photograph, post about, or look up charts you are not caring for.

checks.q: You realize you missed a scheduled two-hour vital sign recheck on a stable patient. What is the correct sequence?
choices: Chart the vitals you would have expected, then take a real set
Take the vitals now and say nothing, since the patient is stable
Wait until shift change and mention it in handoff
Take the vitals immediately, tell the nurse the recheck was missed, and document the actual time obtained
checks.why: Charting numbers you did not obtain is falsification and is the worst option available. Getting a real set now, disclosing the gap, and documenting the true time is the entire fix.

checks.q: A patient you have cared for twice asks for your phone number and suggests meeting after your shift. What is the best response?
choices: Give a number but do not answer, to avoid upsetting them
State clearly that your relationship can only be clinical, then tell your nurse so it is documented
Say yes to keep the interaction calm and ignore it later
Report it to security immediately as an assault
checks.why: A clear, warm boundary plus telling your nurse protects the patient relationship and protects you. Security is the answer for persistent harassment or touching, not for a single question.

checks.q: A resident tells you privately that a nurse made an error and asks you not to mention it. What is your obligation?
choices: Report what you personally observed through the safety reporting process and tell the charge nurse if patient care is affected
Keep the confidence, since it was shared privately
Confront the nurse yourself in front of the team
Post about it anonymously so the department learns
checks.why: Safety information does not become private because someone asked. Report through the process, keep it factual, and route anything affecting current care to the charge nurse now.

lessons.title: What to say: rounding, service recovery and the waiting room
lessons.body:
Most of what patients remember about an emergency department is not the medicine. It is whether anybody told them what was happening. That part is almost entirely scripted, and the scripts are short.

## The shape of every room entry

A useful sequence is acknowledge, introduce, duration, explanation, thank you.

"Mr. Alvarez, good afternoon. I'm Jose, one of the ED techs. I'm going to take your vital signs, which takes about two minutes. Your blood work went to the lab about twenty minutes ago and results usually take around an hour. I'll be back to check on you in about thirty minutes. Is there anything you need first? I can't give you water until the doctor clears it, but I can get you a warm blanket."

That paragraph does five things: it uses their name, identifies you, sets the duration, explains what is pending honestly, and commits to a return.

## Words that work, and words that cost you

| Say | Instead of |
|---|---|
| "I don't know, but I'll find out who does." | "That's not my job." |
| "The provider will go over those results with you." | "Your EKG looks fine." |
| "I can't promise a time, but here's what's pending." | "It shouldn't be much longer." |
| "It's been a long wait, and that's frustrating." | "Everyone has to wait." |
| "Let me get your nurse, and I'll come back either way." | "They must have forgotten about you." |

Never blame another department, another shift, or the patient's own decisions. It never helps and it always travels.

## Service recovery in five moves

When someone is angry, they are almost always angry about time, dignity or pain.

1. **Listen** without interrupting, all the way to the end of the sentence.
2. **Acknowledge the specific thing:** "Four hours in a chair with a migraine is a long time."
3. **Apologize for the experience,** not for a fault you are inventing: "I'm sorry this has been such a long wait."
4. **Fix what is in your reach:** a blanket, an update, a chair for the spouse, a bathroom escort, a fresh set of vitals, dimming the lights.
5. **Escalate** to the charge nurse when the complaint is about care or when your fix is not enough. Then go back and tell the person you did it.

> **Trap:** Defending the department is the instinct and it is always wrong. "We're really busy tonight" tells a patient in pain that their problem is inconvenient.

## The waiting room

Go out on a schedule rather than when someone yells. Say the honest picture: how many critical patients came in, what the current wait looks like for lower-acuity complaints, and that anyone who feels worse should come to the window immediately.

That last sentence is not customer service. A waiting room is a clinical space, and repeat vital signs on waiting patients catch the person whose condition has changed. If a patient in the lobby looks worse than they did an hour ago, that observation goes to the triage or charge nurse immediately, not at the end of your loop.

## Dignity, in small moves

Knock. Ask before pulling a sheet back. Close the curtain fully, not most of the way. Cover a patient during any transport through a hallway. Get to eye level with someone in a bed or a wheelchair. Use the name they ask you to use.

Use a professional interpreter — in person, by phone, or by video — and document the interpreter's identification. Family members, and especially children, are not interpreters. Face a patient who reads lips, and never speak about someone in the third person while standing over them.

> **On shift:** Ask the family to designate one spokesperson, and find a chair for the person who is staying all night. Both cost you nothing and change the entire tone of a twelve-hour visit.
keyPoints: Structure every room entry: acknowledge, introduce, duration, explanation, thank you, with a commitment to return.
Never interpret results, never promise a time, and never blame another department or shift.
Service recovery is listen, acknowledge the specific thing, apologize for the experience, fix what you can, escalate and report back.
Waiting room rounds are a safety function: repeat vitals and report any patient who looks worse to the triage or charge nurse immediately.
Use professional interpreters, never family or children, and document the interpreter identification.

checks.q: A patient's son says loudly that nobody has told them anything for three hours. What is the best first move?
choices: Explain that the department is extremely busy tonight
Listen fully, acknowledge the specific frustration, apologize for the experience, then give an honest status and fix what you can
Tell him the doctor will be in shortly
Refer him to patient relations
checks.why: Defending the department tells the family their problem is inconvenient, and promising the doctor shortly makes a commitment you do not control. Listening and acknowledging first is what defuses it.

checks.q: A Spanish-speaking patient's 12-year-old daughter offers to interpret. What should you do?
choices: Accept, because it is faster and the family is comfortable
Use the daughter for simple questions only
Use a professional interpreter by phone, video or in person, and document the interpreter identification
Use a translation app on your personal phone
checks.why: Minors are never interpreters, and family members filter and edit even with good intentions. Professional interpretation is both a legal requirement and a safety measure, and it gets documented.

checks.q: Why do techs take repeat vital signs on patients still in the waiting room?
choices: To satisfy patient satisfaction scores
Because a waiting room is a clinical space and repeat vitals catch patients who have deteriorated
Because triage vitals are often entered incorrectly
To justify the length of the wait
checks.why: People deteriorate and die in waiting rooms. Scheduled reassessment is a safety function, and any patient who looks worse goes to the triage or charge nurse right away.

lessons.title: The case log method, with ten entries
lessons.body:
A case log turns shifts into knowledge, and it turns knowledge into an application. It only works if it is short enough that you actually do it, and safe enough that it never creates a privacy problem.

## The rules

Write the entry within `24 hours`, while you still remember why it was interesting. Store it somewhere personal, never on a hospital device or account.

Strip identifiers completely: no names, no dates of birth, no record numbers, no dates of service, no addresses, and no detail so unusual that one person is identifiable from it. Never photograph anything, including a monitor or a tracing. Treat even the de-identified log as private — it is a study tool, not material for a story at a party or a post.

## The template

Age range and sex, chief complaint and duration, the vitals that mattered, what you personally did, the workup, the diagnosis, the disposition, and one line on what you learned. Eight fields, about forty words.

## Ten entries

1. `60s M`, chest pressure `40 min` with jaw ache. EKG at `6 min` showed inferior changes; cath lab activated. Learned: why they ran right-sided leads and held nitroglycerin.
2. `20s F`, one-sided lower abdominal pain, pregnancy test positive, `HR 118`. Ultrasound showed ectopic pregnancy; to the operating room. Learned: shoulder pain as referred bleeding.
3. `80s F`, "just weak." Temp `97.4 F`, `HR 96`, `BP 98/60`, lactate `3.4`. Sepsis from a urinary source. Learned: older adults can be afebrile with severe infection, and cultures precede antibiotics.
4. `40s M`, tremor and `BP 186/104`, last drink two days ago. Withdrawal, treated with benzodiazepines and scored on a scale. Learned: withdrawal can kill, and seizures come `12 to 48 hours` in.
5. `5-year-old`, barking cough with stridor at rest. Dexamethasone and nebulized epinephrine. Learned: the stridor eased in the cold air on the walk in, and why we did not touch the throat.
6. `70s M` on apixaban, tripped on a curb, normal neurologic exam. CT showed a small subdural bleed. Learned: anticoagulation turns a minor fall into an admission.
7. `30s F`, asthma, speaking one word at a time. Back-to-back nebulizers and steroids. Learned: severity graded by speech, and a quiet chest is the bad sign.
8. `50s M`, glucose `480`, deep rapid breathing, fruity breath. Diabetic ketoacidosis. Learned: the insulin drip waited for the potassium result, and why.
9. `90s F`, fall with the right leg shortened and rotated outward. Hip fracture. Learned: ask why she fell; a blood pressure medication had been started nine days earlier.
10. `60s M`, cardiac arrest, `22 min` of CPR. End-tidal carbon dioxide `12`, then jumped to `38` with return of pulses. Learned: end-tidal as both a compression quality and a circulation monitor.

> **Key:** The learning line is the whole point. "I did compressions" is a task. "End-tidal carbon dioxide jumped from 12 to 38 and that was the first sign of pulses" is reasoning, and reasoning is what an interviewer remembers.

## Keeping hours as well as cases

Track patient care experience hours separately: date, shift length, running total, and your supervisor's name and contact. Applications ask for a number and a verifier, and reconstructing two years of shifts from memory is miserable.

> **On shift:** Bring three logged cases to an interview in your head, not on paper. Be able to explain what was done and why, admit what you did not understand at the time, and never share a detail that could identify a patient.
keyPoints: Write entries within 24 hours, on a personal device, with every identifier stripped and no photographs ever.
Eight fields: age range and sex, complaint, key vitals, what you did, workup, diagnosis, disposition, one learning line.
The learning line converts a task into reasoning, which is what interviews and evaluations reward.
Track patient care hours separately with dates, totals and a verifier's contact information.
Bring cases to an interview from memory, never on paper, and never with identifiable detail.

checks.q: Which case log entry is both lawful and useful?
choices: Full name, date of visit and diagnosis, so you can remember the case
A photograph of the monitor with the name cropped out
Age range, complaint, key vitals, what you did, the diagnosis, and one line on what you learned
A detailed narrative naming the attending and the exact date
checks.why: Identifiers, dates and photographs all create privacy exposure, and cropping an image does not de-identify it. The de-identified template captures everything you actually need to learn from.

checks.q: What makes the 'what I learned' line the most valuable field?
choices: It turns a list of tasks into clinical reasoning you can explain later
It lengthens the entry for applications
It substitutes for tracking hours
It documents your contribution for the medical record
checks.why: Programs and supervisors can already assume you performed tasks. Being able to explain why a test was ordered or what a number meant is what distinguishes you, and the log is never part of the medical record.

lessons.title: Nights, weekends and holidays
lessons.body:
Nights are not days with fewer people. The physiology is different, the resources are different, and the patients are different.

## Your body at 0400

Core temperature and alertness bottom out between about `0300` and `0500`, and that is when reaction time is slowest and error rates are highest. The most dangerous part of a night shift is usually the drive home.

What helps, in order of effect: a consistent schedule so the body stops renegotiating, a genuinely dark and quiet sleep space with the phone off, caffeine early in the shift and stopped `4 to 6 hours` before you intend to sleep, a `20-minute` nap when policy allows it, bright light at the start of the shift and sunglasses on the drive home so daylight does not tell your brain to wake up. If you are microsleeping at the wheel, pull over and nap or call someone. Nobody has ever been fired for arriving home late.

Eat a real meal and bring it with you, because nothing is open. Hydrate. Move.

## The resources are thinner

Expect some version of this:

- One environmental services worker, or none, so you turn your own rooms.
- Ultrasound and MRI technologists on call from home, adding `30 to 60 minutes`.
- Fewer laboratory staff, so results take longer.
- No social work or case management until morning, so placement problems simply wait.
- Pharmacy off site in some hospitals, with an after-hours override process.
- Fewer consultants in the building and more by phone.
- No transport team, so you move your own patients.

That changes what you promise patients. "We are waiting for a specialist who comes in at eight" is an honest sentence at `0200`.

## The patients are different

Fewer arrive and more of them are sick. There are two predictable waves: one after bars close, bringing intoxication, assaults, overdoses and psychiatric crises; and an early morning one of chest pain, stroke and breathing problems that woke people from sleep. Nursing homes send patients out at shift change. A small crew means every person is load-bearing.

> **Key:** With a skeleton crew, the tech becomes the department's second set of eyes on everyone, not just on a zone. Walk the whole floor, including the hallway beds and the boarders, every hour.

## Safety

Security presence is lighter overnight. Walk to the parking lot with someone. In any room with an intoxicated or agitated patient, keep the exit behind you, stay out of arm's reach, and do not let a patient get between you and the door.

## Weekends and holidays

Clinics and pharmacies are closed, so the ED absorbs everything: medication refills, results that needed a follow-up call, and problems that could have waited until Monday. Knowing which pharmacies are open `24 hours` in your area is genuinely useful information to hand a discharging nurse. With no outpatient follow-up available, more patients get admitted or observed for things that would have gone home on a Tuesday. Add holiday alcohol, family conflict, and a staff roster thinned by time off.

> **On shift:** Night crews are small and they adopt people fast. Restock without being asked, help with every turn and lift, start the coffee, and know where things are. You will also learn more per shift than on days, because there are fewer people competing for every procedure and more room to ask why.
keyPoints: Alertness and reaction time bottom out between 0300 and 0500, and the drive home is the most dangerous part of the shift.
Stop caffeine 4 to 6 hours before intended sleep, keep a consistent schedule, and use sunglasses on the drive home.
Overnight resources are thinner: on-call imaging, slower labs, no case management, and often no environmental services or transport.
Volume falls but acuity rises, with a bar-close wave and an early-morning wave of cardiac and neurologic complaints.
With a skeleton crew, walk the entire department hourly including hallway beds and boarders, and keep the exit behind you with agitated patients.

checks.q: It is 0300 and a patient needs an ultrasound that is not available until the technologist drives in. What is the appropriate thing to tell the patient?
choices: That the test will happen shortly
That the ultrasound technologist is on call from home and it will be roughly 30 to 60 minutes, and you will update them
Nothing, since the nurse will handle it
That the department is too busy for the test right now
checks.why: Honest, specific information about an on-call resource is both accurate and reassuring. Vague promises you do not control are what generate complaints an hour later.

checks.q: Which combination best protects a tech during an overnight shift?
choices: Extra caffeine at 0500 and a fast drive home
Skipping breaks so the shift passes faster
A consistent sleep schedule, caffeine stopped 4 to 6 hours before sleep, and pulling over to nap if drowsy while driving
Working straight through and sleeping in the car with the engine running
checks.why: Late caffeine wrecks the sleep that actually restores you, and drowsy driving after a night shift is a leading cause of injury in this workforce. Schedule consistency does more than any single trick.

cards.front: What is the correct order of steps when rooming a patient?
cards.back: Two identifiers, gown and undress, belongings inventory, monitor and correctly sized cuff, full vitals with pain and temperature, set the room and call bell, then say what happens next.

cards.front: Which patients must be undressed and gowned at rooming?
cards.back: Chest pain, abdominal pain, trauma, syncope, weakness, fever without a source, any possible rash, and any diabetic foot complaint. You cannot assess what you cannot see. Cover them immediately afterward.

cards.front: Why does a blood pressure cuff that is too small give a wrong reading?
cards.back: A small bladder needs extra pressure to occlude the artery, so it reads falsely high. The bladder should wrap about 80 percent of the arm circumference.

cards.front: How should dentures, hearing aids and glasses be handled?
cards.back: Labeled containers, recorded on the belongings inventory, never wrapped in a towel or left on a meal tray. That is how they reach the linen chute and become a hospital claim.

cards.front: What should the walk to the door screen for at discharge?
cards.back: An unsteady gait, a low walking saturation, ongoing intoxication, no ride, no coat in cold weather, and no plan. Report anything you find to the nurse before the patient leaves.

cards.front: What are the steps of a quick room turn, and which one gets forgotten?
cards.back: Strip linens, disinfect stretcher and cables, remake, restock, rehang the cuff and probe, lower the bed, call bell in reach. The forgotten step is marking the bed available in the tracking system.

cards.front: How long do a quick turn and a terminal clean take?
cards.back: About 5 to 10 minutes for a quick turn and 20 to 30 minutes for a terminal clean. Rooms with contact precautions require the full environmental services clean with the specified agent.

cards.front: Why does disinfectant contact time matter?
cards.back: The surface must stay visibly wet for the time on the label, often 1 to 4 minutes, or the organisms survive. Wiping a surface dry in fifteen seconds accomplishes nothing.

cards.front: When should the patient be moved during an EMS handoff?
cards.back: After the verbal report, unless the patient needs immediate intervention. Transfer on an agreed count, keep oxygen and monitoring continuous, switch monitors last, and note the time.

cards.front: What four elements structure a prehospital report?
cards.back: Mechanism or complaint with the time of onset, injuries or findings, signs including vitals with times, and treatment given with the response.

cards.front: Why is the first prehospital blood pressure worth writing down immediately?
cards.back: It exists only with the crew. A patient arriving at 104/60 after fluids looks different once you know they were 72/40 in the driveway, and nobody can reconstruct it later.

cards.front: What must you capture from EMS for any neurologic complaint?
cards.back: The last known well time plus the name and phone number of the person who witnessed it. Thrombolytic and thrombectomy eligibility runs entirely on that clock.

cards.front: Which scene details should a tech preserve from a crew?
cards.back: How and where the patient was found, position, blood loss at scene, pill bottles or a note, home conditions, who was present, and helmet or seatbelt use. That information existed for four minutes.

cards.front: What are the tech's three fallback questions for a thin EMS report?
cards.back: What was the first blood pressure, when did this start or when were they last normal, and did they receive anything from you?

cards.front: Does a prehospital 12-lead replace the one you do on arrival?
cards.back: No. Repeat the EKG on arrival for chest pain and get it into a provider's hands within 10 minutes of arrival. The prehospital tracing is added to the chart, not substituted for yours.

cards.front: What equipment must be present and working in every ED room?
cards.back: Wall suction with canister, tubing and rigid tip; wall oxygen with flowmeter, cannula, nonrebreather and bag-valve mask; a monitor with leads, pulse oximetry and cuffs in at least three sizes; sharps container and supplies.

cards.front: What is the order of draw for blood tubes?
cards.back: Blood cultures, light blue citrate, gold or red serum, green heparin, lavender EDTA, gray fluoride. The order prevents additive carryover from falsifying potassium and clotting results.

cards.front: How is a crash cart organized?
cards.back: Monitor-defibrillator, pads and backboard on top; then drawers for airway, circulation and access, medications, and procedures. It is sealed with a numbered breakaway tag matched to a log.

cards.front: What does a per-shift crash cart check cover?
cards.back: Tag intact with the number matching the log, defibrillator self-test passed and battery charged, suction working, portable oxygen above about 1,500 psi, and no expired items on the exterior.

cards.front: Which three failures stop a resuscitation before it starts?
cards.back: No suction, a dead defibrillator battery, and an empty oxygen cylinder. Check all three in every resus bay at the start of every shift; it takes about ninety seconds.

cards.front: Which specialty carts should you be able to find without looking?
cards.back: Difficult airway, central line, chest tube, lumbar puncture, pelvic and precipitous delivery, laceration, splinting, burn, eye tray, and the pediatric cart with its length-based tape.

cards.front: What are the two local rules to learn before sending your first specimen?
cards.back: Which specimens are never sent through the pneumatic tube system, and that nothing leaves the bedside without a label. An unlabeled specimen is discarded and the patient gets stuck again.

cards.front: Why restock in the moment rather than at the end of a task?
cards.back: Thirty seconds now replaces four minutes at 0300 when someone else opens an empty drawer during an emergency. The resus bay in particular is restocked before anything else.

cards.front: What are the tech's priorities in a stroke alert?
cards.back: Last known well time with a witness contact, immediate glucose, a measured weight in kilograms, vitals and 12-lead, access and labs if credentialed, nothing by mouth, and no delay to CT.

cards.front: Why is a glucose check the first thing in a stroke alert?
cards.back: Hypoglycemia mimics a stroke exactly, including one-sided weakness and speech loss, and it is correctable in about ninety seconds. Missing it sends a treatable patient into the scanner.

cards.front: What are the door-to-CT and door-to-needle targets for stroke?
cards.back: About 25 minutes from door to CT and 60 minutes from door to thrombolytic, with many centers aiming for 45. Labs and IV access travel with the patient rather than delaying the scan.

cards.front: How is clothing handled in a trauma alert involving an assault?
cards.back: Cut along the seams, never through holes in the fabric, and place items in paper bags rather than plastic so evidence is preserved and moisture does not degrade it.

cards.front: Why do blankets go back on a trauma patient as soon as the exam is done?
cards.back: Hypothermia impairs clotting and worsens bleeding. The room is cold for the staff, not the patient, and warming is part of the resuscitation.

cards.front: What are the compression standards you are expected to hit in a code?
cards.back: 100 to 120 per minute, at least 2 inches deep, full recoil, interruptions under 10 seconds, switching compressors every 2 minutes.

cards.front: What does end-tidal carbon dioxide tell you during a resuscitation?
cards.back: Above about 10 mmHg suggests compressions are producing adequate flow. A sudden rise to 35 to 40 often signals return of spontaneous circulation before you can feel a pulse.

cards.front: What must be set up before any drug is given for procedural sedation?
cards.back: Continuous monitoring with pulse oximetry and end-tidal carbon dioxide, oxygen, tested suction, a bag-valve mask at the head, the airway cart in the room, and a dedicated person recording vitals.

cards.front: What are the discharge criteria after procedural sedation?
cards.back: Back to baseline mental status, protecting the airway, stable vital signs, ambulating if appropriate, and a responsible adult to accompany them. No driving for 24 hours.

cards.front: What does a tech do to speed a consult?
cards.back: Have the patient gowned, specimens already collected, tracings on the chart and family present, and tell the nurse the moment the consultant arrives. Preparation converts a forty-minute consult into ten.

cards.front: What are the six steps between an admission decision and the patient leaving?
cards.back: Decision to admit, choosing the service, calling the accepting provider, writing admission orders, bed request and assignment, and nurse-to-nurse report. Each step is a waiting point.

cards.front: What do the different inpatient bed levels mean?
cards.back: Medical-surgical for routine care, telemetry for continuous cardiac monitoring, step-down for higher needs, and intensive care for the sickest. The level is a monitoring decision, not a comfort one.

cards.front: What care does a boarding admitted patient still need from you?
cards.back: The full rounding loop: scheduled vitals, toileting, repositioning about every 2 hours to protect skin, meals if ordered, oral care, and the same attention as a new patient.

cards.front: What does EMTALA require when transferring a patient to another hospital?
cards.back: Stabilize within your capability, obtain an accepting physician and facility, document risks and benefits, send the medical record, and use an appropriate level of transport.

cards.front: What belongs in a transfer packet?
cards.back: Printed chart and orders, EKG tracings, imaging pushed electronically or burned to a disc, the transfer form, and the patient's belongings. Anything omitted arrives hours later by fax, if at all.

cards.front: What is the number for poison control, and when is it used?
cards.back: 1-800-222-1222, for any ingestion, exposure or overdose question. It is a consult like any other and the provider or nurse makes the call.

cards.front: How do you handle a colleague who is repeatedly rude to you?
cards.back: Separate a bad moment from a pattern. Address a pattern once, privately and specifically, then escalate to charge and the educator or manager. Never return it and never argue where patients can hear.

cards.front: How should you communicate with a provider who is curt and overloaded?
cards.back: Lead with the ask in one sentence and pick a moment when they are not mid-thought. Save any concern about demeaning behavior for a private conversation or your supervisor.

cards.front: What is the five-step sequence after you make a mistake?
cards.back: Patient first with a reassessment, tell the nurse immediately, document objectively with no blame, file the incident or safety report including near-misses, and ask what to change.

cards.front: What do you say when a patient asks you out?
cards.back: Be warm, clear and non-negotiable: you are here as their tech and that is the only relationship possible. Then tell your nurse so it is documented and you are not alone with it.

cards.front: When does a patient's behavior stop being awkward and start being reportable?
cards.back: Persistent sexual comments, deliberate exposure, or any touching. Step out of the room, get help, and report it through the department's process. It is not part of the job.

cards.front: How do you decline an out-of-scope request without friction?
cards.back: Offer the part you can do and hand off the part you cannot: 'I'm not signed off on that, but I'll set it all up and grab the nurse.' Never debate it in front of a patient.

cards.front: What are the absolute privacy rules for a tech?
cards.back: No photographs ever, no looking up your own chart or a family member's or a coworker's, no discussing patients in elevators or the cafeteria, and no posting about shifts even with names removed.

cards.front: What is the shape of a good room entry?
cards.back: Acknowledge by name, introduce yourself and your role, say how long this will take, explain what is pending honestly, thank them, and commit to a return time you can keep.

cards.front: Give three replacements for phrases that cost you credibility.
cards.back: 'I don't know, but I'll find out who does' replaces 'not my job.' 'The provider will go over those results' replaces interpreting. 'Here's what's pending' replaces 'it shouldn't be much longer.'

cards.front: What are the five moves of service recovery?
cards.back: Listen without interrupting, acknowledge the specific frustration, apologize for the experience, fix what is in your reach, and escalate to charge when needed, then report back that you did.

cards.front: Why is 'we're really busy tonight' the wrong thing to say?
cards.back: It tells a patient in pain that their problem is inconvenient, and it defends the department instead of addressing the person. Acknowledge the wait itself instead.

cards.front: Why are waiting room rounds a clinical duty rather than customer service?
cards.back: Patients deteriorate and die in waiting rooms. Scheduled updates and repeat vitals catch the person who has worsened, and any change goes to the triage or charge nurse immediately.

cards.front: What are the rules for interpreters?
cards.back: Use a professional interpreter in person, by phone or by video, and document the interpreter identification. Family members filter, and minors are never interpreters.

cards.front: Name five small dignity moves in a patient room.
cards.back: Knock before entering, ask before pulling back a sheet, close the curtain fully, cover the patient for any hallway transport, and get to eye level using the name they prefer.

cards.front: What are the privacy rules for a personal case log?
cards.back: Write within 24 hours on a personal device, strip names, dates of birth, record numbers, dates of service and any uniquely identifying detail, and never photograph anything.

cards.front: What eight fields make up a case log entry?
cards.back: Age range and sex, chief complaint and duration, the vitals that mattered, what you personally did, the workup, the diagnosis, the disposition, and one line on what you learned.

cards.front: Why is the learning line the most important field?
cards.back: It converts a task list into reasoning. 'I did compressions' is a task; 'end-tidal carbon dioxide jumped from 12 to 38 and that was the first sign of pulses' is understanding.

cards.front: What should you track alongside cases for applications?
cards.back: Patient care experience hours: dates, shift length, a running total, and a supervisor's name and contact for verification. Reconstructing two years of shifts later is miserable.

cards.front: How do you use your case log in an interview?
cards.back: Bring three cases in your head rather than on paper, explain what was done and why, be honest about what you did not understand at the time, and share no identifying detail.

cards.front: Give an example of a well-formed case log entry.
cards.back: 80s F, weakness. Temp 97.4 F, HR 96, BP 98/60, lactate 3.4. Urinary sepsis, admitted. Learned: older adults are often afebrile with severe infection, and cultures come before antibiotics.

cards.front: When is a night shift worker at the highest risk of error?
cards.back: Between about 0300 and 0500, when core temperature and alertness bottom out. The most dangerous single part of the shift is usually the drive home.

cards.front: What are the highest-yield night shift countermeasures?
cards.back: A consistent schedule, a dark quiet sleep space, caffeine early and stopped 4 to 6 hours before sleep, a 20-minute nap where allowed, bright light at shift start and sunglasses driving home.

cards.front: Which resources are thinner overnight?
cards.back: Environmental services, transport, ultrasound and MRI technologists on call from home, fewer lab staff, no case management or social work, off-site pharmacy, and more consultants by phone.

cards.front: What are the two predictable overnight patient waves?
cards.back: A bar-close wave of intoxication, assaults, overdoses and psychiatric crises, and an early-morning wave of chest pain, stroke and breathing problems that woke people from sleep.

cards.front: How do you stay physically safe on a night shift?
cards.back: Walk to the parking lot with someone, keep the exit behind you in any room with an agitated or intoxicated patient, stay out of arm's reach, and never let a patient get between you and the door.

quiz.q: You are rooming a 66-year-old man with dizziness and weakness. He is fully dressed in long pants and a heavy sweater. What should you do?
choices: Leave him dressed to keep him warm and take vitals over the sleeve
Undress and gown him while keeping him covered, then obtain vitals and a glucose
Ask the nurse whether a gown is necessary
Gown him only if the provider requests it
quiz.why: Weakness can hide a rash, a pressure injury, a gastrointestinal bleed on the linens, or a diabetic foot infection, and vitals taken over clothing are unreliable. Dignity is preserved by covering, not by leaving him dressed.

quiz.q: A 24-year-old woman arrives with right lower abdominal pain. Which anticipatory tech action is most valuable at rooming?
choices: Collect a urine specimen, since the pregnancy result shapes both the differential and the imaging choice
Apply continuous cardiac monitoring
Obtain a 12-lead EKG
Set up a suture tray
quiz.why: In anyone of childbearing potential, appendicitis and ectopic pregnancy sit on the same differential, and the pregnancy test gates ultrasound versus CT. A specimen collected at rooming can save an hour.

quiz.q: You are wheeling a discharged 80-year-old to the door at 0215 when she tells you her ride is not answering and she has no money for a cab. What do you do?
choices: Call her a cab and let her settle the bill later
Leave her in the lobby to keep calling
Walk her to the bus stop and wait with her
Stop the discharge at the door and tell the nurse, so case management resources or a hospital transport option can be arranged
quiz.why: A discharge is not complete until the patient can actually leave safely. Techs are often the last person to learn this, and saying it before she is out the door is the entire intervention.

quiz.q: You cleaned and restocked room 9 in seven minutes but did not update the tracking system. The charge nurse says there are no beds. What happened?
choices: The room requires an environmental services signature to count
Nothing; charge will check the room physically
The board still lists the bed as unavailable, so a waiting patient cannot be assigned to it
The computer removes rooms after a set interval
quiz.why: Flow runs on the board. A clean room the system shows as dirty is invisible during bed assignment, and the waiting room keeps growing while an empty bed sits there.

quiz.q: EMS arrives with an unstable patient and begins a verbal report. Two staff members start to move the patient onto the ED stretcher mid-sentence. What is the correct practice?
choices: Complete the report first unless immediate intervention is required, then transfer on a count with oxygen and monitoring continuous
Move first, then ask the crew to repeat everything
Have the crew write it down instead of speaking
Let the physician take the report separately afterward
quiz.why: Information given during a transfer is lost, and the details most often lost are the ones only the crew has. The move is done deliberately after the report, with monitoring uninterrupted.

quiz.q: A patient arrives by EMS with slurred speech that began 'sometime this morning.' The neighbor who found him is about to leave. What is the highest-value action?
choices: Ask the neighbor for insurance information
Let the neighbor leave and obtain history from the patient later
Get the last known well time from the neighbor and write down the neighbor's phone number before he leaves
Ask the crew to estimate the onset time
quiz.why: Thrombolytic and thrombectomy windows run from when the patient was last normal. If the only witness walks out unrecorded, the team may be unable to establish eligibility at all.

quiz.q: A crew reports a blood pressure of 108/64 on arrival for a patient with a gastrointestinal bleed. What question should the tech ask?
choices: Which hospital usually takes these patients
What was the first blood pressure you obtained, and what did you give?
Did the patient walk to the ambulance
How long was the transport
quiz.why: The number on arrival may reflect prehospital fluids. A first pressure of 72/40 at the scene changes the entire interpretation, and only the crew has it.

quiz.q: A chest pain patient arrives with a prehospital 12-lead performed nine minutes ago. What should the tech do?
choices: Nothing, since an EKG was already obtained
Wait for the provider to request one
Obtain a repeat EKG only if the pain changes
Obtain a new 12-lead on arrival and get it to a provider within 10 minutes of arrival, adding the prehospital tracing to the chart
quiz.why: The door-to-EKG clock starts at your door, and findings evolve minute to minute. The prehospital tracing is valuable for comparison, not a substitute.

quiz.q: You are drawing a rainbow of tubes plus blood cultures on a septic patient. What is the correct order?
choices: Lavender, gold, light blue, cultures, gray
Gray, green, gold, lavender, cultures
Blood cultures, light blue, gold or red, green, lavender, gray
Any order, provided each tube is filled to the fill line
quiz.why: Cultures come first to minimize contamination, and the remaining sequence prevents additive carryover that produces falsely abnormal potassium and clotting results.

quiz.q: At the start of a night shift, which check on the resuscitation bay matters most?
choices: Linen and pillow stock
Computer login and chair position
Wall art and curtain condition
Suction working, defibrillator self-test passed with a charged battery, oxygen cylinder pressure adequate, crash cart tag intact and matching the log
quiz.why: Those are the failures that stop a resuscitation before it begins. Everything else can be improvised mid-code; none of these can.

quiz.q: You send a urine specimen to the lab and it is discarded. The most likely reason is:
choices: It was unlabeled or labeled away from the bedside, so identity could not be confirmed
The lab was short-staffed
The container was the wrong color
The order had not yet been entered
quiz.why: Unlabeled and mislabeled specimens are discarded as a patient safety rule, and the consequence is another collection or another needle stick. Labels go on at the bedside with two identifiers.

quiz.q: Which item would you expect to find in the airway drawer of a crash cart rather than elsewhere?
choices: Intraosseous drill
Bougie and laryngoscope blades
Amiodarone
Chest tube tray
quiz.why: Airway holds laryngoscopy equipment, tubes, stylets, bougies, supraglottic airways and carbon dioxide detection. The drill belongs to circulation and access, amiodarone to medications, and the chest tube to procedures.

quiz.q: A stroke alert patient is ready for CT but you have not drawn labs or started an IV. What is correct?
choices: Go to CT now; labs and access can happen en route or afterward
Draw labs and place two IVs first
Wait for the neurologist to examine the patient
Complete a full head-to-toe assessment first
quiz.why: The door-to-CT target of about 25 minutes drives everything that follows. Doing a useful task at the wrong moment is the single most common tech error in a stroke alert.

quiz.q: A patient with sudden right-sided weakness and slurred speech has a glucose of 38 mg/dL. What is the significance?
choices: It is incidental and the stroke workup continues unchanged
Hypoglycemia can mimic a stroke exactly, and correcting it may resolve the deficits entirely
It confirms the stroke diagnosis
It means a thrombolytic will simply be given at a lower dose
quiz.why: This is precisely why glucose is the first tech task in a stroke alert. A correctable metabolic cause can reproduce focal deficits, and treating it takes under two minutes.

quiz.q: A trauma patient's clothing must be removed. He was stabbed through his shirt. How should you proceed?
choices: Cut through the stab hole for speed and place clothing in a plastic bag
Pull the shirt off over his head
Cut along the seams avoiding the hole, and place the clothing in a paper bag
Leave the shirt on until police arrive
quiz.why: Cutting through a defect destroys evidence, and plastic traps moisture that degrades it. Paper bags and seam cuts preserve both the evidence and the patient's access to care.

quiz.q: During a cardiac arrest, end-tidal carbon dioxide suddenly rises from 14 to 39 mmHg. What does this most likely indicate?
choices: The airway has become dislodged
Compressions have become too shallow
The capnography sensor has failed
Return of spontaneous circulation, which should prompt a rhythm and pulse check at the next appropriate pause
quiz.why: A sharp rise reflects restored pulmonary blood flow carrying carbon dioxide to the lungs. Dislodgement or failing compressions drive the number down, not up.

quiz.q: During procedural sedation for a shoulder reduction, the patient begins snoring and the saturation drifts from 99 to 92 percent. What should the tech do?
choices: Silence the alarm and watch for another minute
Announce it immediately to the provider and nurse while repositioning the airway as directed
Step out to find the respiratory therapist
Increase the oxygen flow without telling anyone
quiz.why: Snoring is partial obstruction and a drifting saturation is an early warning during sedation. Saying it out loud at once is the reason a dedicated observer is in the room, and oxygen changes are not a tech action.

quiz.q: A patient has been waiting three hours for an admission bed. What is the most useful thing the tech can do?
choices: Call patient flow directly to demand a bed
Explain that the delay is the inpatient unit's fault
Continue the full rounding loop: scheduled vitals, toileting, repositioning about every 2 hours, meals if ordered, and updates
Nothing, since the inpatient team now owns this patient
quiz.why: Boarders remain ED patients until they physically leave, and they are the group most likely to fall, develop pressure injuries, or deteriorate unnoticed. Bed assignment is not a tech function and blaming another unit helps nobody.

quiz.q: A consultant arrives to see a patient in room 12. What should the tech do?
choices: Tell the patient's nurse immediately that the consultant is at the bedside
Give the consultant a verbal summary of the patient's course
Interpret the pending lab results for the consultant
Leave the area so the consultation is private
quiz.why: The nurse needs to be present or aware for orders and decisions that follow. Summaries and result interpretation belong to the nurse and provider, not to the tech.

quiz.q: A patient with severe burns is being transferred to a burn center. Which part of the process is the tech most responsible for?
choices: Obtaining the accepting physician's agreement
Explaining the risks and benefits of transfer to the patient
Selecting the level of transport
Assembling the transfer packet: printed record, EKGs, imaging, transfer form and belongings
quiz.why: Physician acceptance, the risk discussion and transport level are provider and nurse responsibilities under EMTALA. The record packet is the piece that predictably gets left behind, and preventing that is a tech task.

quiz.q: A family asks why their mother is in 'observation' rather than being admitted. What is the correct response?
choices: Explain that observation means she is not sick enough to be admitted
Tell them the provider or nurse will explain what observation status means for her care
Explain the billing difference between observation and inpatient status
Tell them it is only a paperwork difference and means nothing
quiz.why: Status decisions carry clinical and financial implications a tech is not positioned to explain, and a careless answer can cause real harm. Route the question to the nurse or provider.

quiz.q: You mislabeled a blood tube and realize it after it was sent. What is the correct sequence?
choices: Call the lab and ask them to change the name on the specimen
Wait for the result and see whether it looks plausible
Correct the electronic record to match the specimen
Tell the nurse immediately, have the specimen cancelled, redraw with two identifiers, and file the safety report
quiz.why: A mislabeled specimen can assign one patient's result to another, which is among the most dangerous errors in a hospital. Labels are never edited after the fact; the specimen is cancelled and redrawn.

quiz.q: A senior tech tells you to chart a set of vital signs for a patient you did not assess, saying 'they were fine an hour ago.' What do you do?
choices: Chart them, since a senior colleague directed it
Chart them but note the source
Decline, obtain a real set of vitals now, and chart the actual time obtained
Ignore the request and say nothing
quiz.why: Charting observations you did not make is falsification, regardless of who asked. Going and getting a real set takes two minutes and resolves the problem entirely.

quiz.q: A patient repeatedly makes sexual comments to you and grabs your arm as you take vitals. What is the correct response?
choices: Step out of the room, tell your nurse and charge nurse, and report it through the department's process
Tolerate it because the patient is ill
Respond with a joke to keep the interaction light
Refuse to provide any further care to the patient without explanation
quiz.why: Harassment is not part of the job, and reporting it is the professional response rather than an overreaction. Care continues, with a chaperone or a reassignment arranged through the charge nurse.

quiz.q: You are curious about a coworker who was treated in your ED last week and her chart is one click away. What applies?
choices: Access is acceptable because you both work there
Accessing a chart you are not caring for is a privacy violation, and access is audited
It is permitted if you do not tell anyone
It is permitted if you were on shift that day
quiz.why: Access is limited to a legitimate care need, and audit logs make casual access traceable. Looking up coworkers, family members, or your own chart through the clinical system is a common and career-ending mistake.

quiz.q: A patient's son says loudly that nobody has updated them in three hours. What is the best opening move?
choices: Explain how busy the department is tonight
Listen fully, acknowledge the specific frustration, apologize for the experience, then give an honest status
Promise that the doctor will be in within ten minutes
Direct him to patient relations
