quiz.why: Defending the department signals that his concern is inconvenient, and promising a physician's arrival commits to something you do not control. Listening and acknowledging first is what actually lowers the temperature.

quiz.q: A patient asks whether his CT showed anything. You saw a result flagged on the board. What do you say?
choices: Tell him the result but add that the provider will confirm
Tell him it looked normal to you
Tell him you cannot see results
Tell him the provider will go over the results with him, and let the nurse know he is asking
quiz.why: Interpreting results is outside scope and risks being both wrong and harmful. Saying you cannot see results is untrue; the accurate and useful answer routes the question and flags the need for an update.

quiz.q: During waiting room rounds you find a patient triaged two hours ago for abdominal pain who is now pale, sweaty and slumped in the chair. What do you do?
choices: Finish rounding on the remaining patients, then report it
Offer him water and recheck in 20 minutes
Notify the triage or charge nurse immediately and obtain a repeat set of vital signs
Move him to a room yourself without telling anyone
quiz.why: Waiting room rounds exist to catch deterioration, and the finding is worthless if it waits until the end of the loop. Moving a patient into a bed is a charge nurse decision, and food or water may be contraindicated.

quiz.q: A Portuguese-speaking patient's adult son offers to interpret for a discharge conversation. What is correct?
choices: Use a professional interpreter and document the interpreter identification
Use the son, since he is an adult and consents
Use a translation app on a personal phone
Proceed in English and use gestures
quiz.why: Family members edit and summarize even with good intentions, and interpretation is both a legal requirement and a safety measure. Professional interpretation is available by phone or video around the clock and gets documented.

quiz.q: Which case log entry is both compliant and useful?
choices: Patient's full name, visit date and the attending's name, with the diagnosis
A cropped photograph of the patient's monitor
70s M on apixaban, mechanical fall with normal neuro exam, CT showed small subdural, admitted. Learned: anticoagulation changes a minor fall
A detailed narrative naming the ambulance crew and the exact time of arrival
quiz.why: Names, dates, staff identities and photographs all create privacy exposure, and cropping an image does not de-identify it. The de-identified entry with a learning line carries everything you actually need.

quiz.q: In a PA school interview you are asked to describe a memorable patient. What is the strongest approach?
choices: Describe a de-identified case from memory, explaining what was done and why, and what you learned
Read the entry aloud from your written log
Describe the case with the date and hospital so it sounds credible
Avoid clinical cases entirely and describe only your duties
quiz.why: Reasoning is what distinguishes an applicant, and identifying details are both unnecessary and a privacy risk. Bringing the log itself into an interview is a mistake; bring the understanding instead.

quiz.q: At 0300 a patient needs an ultrasound and the technologist is on call from home. What should you tell the patient?
choices: That the study will be done shortly
Nothing, since the nurse handles updates
That the department is too busy right now
That the technologist is coming in from home and it will be roughly 30 to 60 minutes, and that you will check back
quiz.why: Honest specifics about an on-call resource reassure a patient far more than a vague promise you cannot keep. Silence produces the complaint an hour later.

quiz.q: You finish a night shift at 0730 and feel your eyes closing on the highway. What is the correct action?
choices: Open the windows and turn up the radio
Pull over and nap, or arrange another ride home
Drink more coffee and continue driving
Drive faster to shorten the exposure
quiz.why: Drowsy driving after night shifts is a leading cause of serious injury in this workforce, and stimulation tricks do not restore alertness. A twenty-minute nap or a ride is the only reliable fix.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes overnight and holiday ED operations?
choices: Volume and acuity both fall, so the shift is easier
Staffing matches daytime levels because acuity is higher
Volume falls while average acuity rises, and support services such as imaging, case management and environmental services are reduced or on call
Consultants respond faster overnight because they have fewer patients
quiz.why: Fewer patients arrive but a larger share are seriously ill, while the resources that resolve them are thinner. That combination is exactly why each staff member carries more of the department overnight.

scenarios.title: 0310: the boarder nobody is watching
scenarios.intro: 0310 on a night shift. Eleven patients in the department and six of them are admitted boarders waiting for inpatient beds. You are the only tech on. Hallway bed 3 holds a 78-year-old woman admitted six hours ago for pneumonia; the medical floor has not called for report. Her daughter went home at midnight. The last documented vital signs are from 2140.

steps.prompt: You are walking the department on your hourly loop. Hallway bed 3 is turned toward the wall. The blanket is on the floor, the call bell is looped over the IV pole out of reach, and she is breathing faster than you remember.

choices.text: Take a full set of vitals, put the call bell in her hand, reposition her, and report the change to her nurse using who, what changed, what you did, what you need
choices.feedback: Correct. Boarders are the most likely patients in the department to deteriorate unnoticed. A full set plus a structured report is exactly the intervention.

choices.text: Note that she is admitted and leave her for the inpatient team
choices.feedback: Wrong. Until she physically leaves, she is an ED patient and she is yours. This is how boarders come to harm.

choices.text: Pick up the blanket and move on, since she is sleeping
choices.feedback: Insufficient. A respiratory rate of 26 with a saturation of 91 percent in a pneumonia patient is a change, not sleep.

choices.text: Apply oxygen at 2 L/min to bring the saturation up, then tell the nurse
choices.feedback: Out of scope. Oxygen is a medication and starting or changing it is a nursing decision. Get the vitals and get the nurse.

steps.prompt: The nurse is in a room with a patient in restraints and cannot step out for several minutes. She asks you to keep an eye on the patient.

choices.text: Tell the charge nurse now, giving the same structured report, since the nurse is committed elsewhere
choices.feedback: Correct. When your nurse is unreachable and something is getting worse, charge is the next stop. That is what charge is for.

choices.text: Wait outside the restrained patient's room until your nurse is free
choices.feedback: Too passive. The trend is moving in the wrong direction and waiting costs time you do not have.

choices.text: Recheck the vitals in fifteen minutes and escalate if worse
choices.feedback: The saturation is already falling. Reassessment is good, but escalation should not wait on another data point here.

choices.text: Move her from the hallway into an empty room yourself
choices.feedback: Bed movement is a charge nurse decision, and moving a deteriorating patient alone without telling anyone makes her harder to find.

steps.prompt: The charge nurse comes immediately, listens to her chest, and starts oxygen. She asks you to get a 12-lead, a repeat set with a manual pressure, and to call the lab for a recheck of the blood cultures drawn earlier.

choices.text: Do the EKG first, then the manual pressure, then the phone call, and say out loud when each is done
choices.feedback: Correct. Sequence by what changes decisions fastest, and close every loop out loud so nobody has to check on you.

choices.text: Make the phone call first because it is quickest
choices.feedback: The phone call changes nothing in the next ten minutes. The tracing and the pressure might.

choices.text: Delegate the EKG to the unit clerk so you can do the vitals
choices.feedback: The clerk is not credentialed to obtain a 12-lead. Do the clinical tasks yourself and use the clerk for the phone.

choices.text: Do everything at once by starting the EKG while asking the clerk to call the lab
choices.feedback: Reasonable use of the clerk, as long as you personally own the tracing and the manual pressure.

steps.prompt: Things stabilize. The charge nurse asks you to document what you found and what you did. The last documented vitals before yours were from 2140, more than five hours earlier.

choices.text: Document your vitals with the actual times obtained, your observations, and the time you notified the nurse and charge nurse, without characterizing anyone's earlier care
choices.feedback: Correct. Facts, times and notifications. The five-hour documentation gap is a real finding, and a safety report is the place it gets addressed.

choices.text: Backfill estimated vitals for the missing hours so the record looks continuous
choices.feedback: Falsification, and a serious one. Never chart observations you did not make.

choices.text: Write that the previous shift neglected the patient
choices.feedback: A conclusion, not an observation. Document what you found and when; blame belongs nowhere in a chart.

choices.text: Document your findings and also file a safety report about the five-hour gap in boarder monitoring
choices.feedback: Good. The system problem is that boarders are not on a rounding schedule, and that only gets fixed if somebody reports it.

steps.prompt: It is 0700 and you are handing off to the day tech.

choices.text: Go bed by bed: who is in each, what is pending, what is due and when, who is a fall risk or a boarder needing repositioning, and specifically flag hallway bed 3 and the overnight events
choices.feedback: Correct. The 0700 handoff is the most dangerous transition of the day, and boarders are exactly what falls through it.

choices.text: Tell the day tech the department is quiet and leave
choices.feedback: The department is not quiet; it holds six boarders and a patient who deteriorated overnight. A handoff is a safety event, not a courtesy.

choices.text: Write a note at the desk instead of speaking, since you are past your shift end
choices.feedback: A written note is better than nothing, but it does not let the incoming tech ask questions. Stay the four minutes.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: boarders belong to the ED until they physically leave, and they are the patients most likely to deteriorate with nobody watching. An hourly loop that includes hallway beds is what catches it. Report changes in a structure a busy nurse can act on, escalate to charge when your nurse is committed, keep clinical tasks with credentialed hands, document facts and notification times rather than conclusions, and file the safety report when the real problem is that nobody was scheduled to look.

scenarios.title: Hour four in the waiting room
scenarios.intro: 1840 on a Sunday. Twenty-six people in the waiting room, two trauma activations in the last hour, and every bed is full with four boarders. You have been assigned to the lobby for waiting room rounds: repeat vital signs, updates, and eyes on everybody. The charge nurse says the current wait for lower-acuity complaints is about three and a half hours.

steps.prompt: A man stands up and says loudly, to the room as much as to you, that his wife has been sitting here for four hours with a migraine while 'people who came in after us went back.' Several people look up.

choices.text: Let him finish, acknowledge the specific frustration, apologize for the experience, then explain triage by danger and say what you can do right now
choices.feedback: Correct. Listen, acknowledge the actual thing, apologize for the experience rather than inventing a fault, then act. All five service recovery moves in one exchange.

choices.text: Explain that the department is extremely busy tonight
choices.feedback: Defensive. It tells a person in pain that her problem is inconvenient, and it is the most common wrong instinct in this situation.

choices.text: Tell him she will be called back shortly
choices.feedback: A promise you do not control. When it does not happen in twenty minutes, you have converted frustration into distrust.

choices.text: Direct him to patient relations and continue rounding
choices.feedback: Escalating a complaint has its place, but not before you have listened or offered anything you could actually do.

steps.prompt: He calms slightly. His wife is sitting with her eyes closed under the fluorescent lights, hood up, with a vomit bag in her lap.

choices.text: Take a repeat set of vitals, offer a quieter corner or an eye mask, a fresh emesis bag and a blanket, and tell the triage nurse she is still vomiting
choices.feedback: Correct. Small comfort measures you control plus a reassessment reported to triage is the whole of what a tech can offer here, and it is a lot.

choices.text: Tell him she cannot have anything until she is seen
choices.feedback: Technically about food and medication, but you have just refused things you could actually provide, like darkness, a blanket and a clean bag.

choices.text: Move her to a bed yourself because she looks uncomfortable
choices.feedback: Bed assignment is the charge nurse's decision. Report what you see and let them make it.

choices.text: Offer her water and crackers while she waits
choices.feedback: Do not. She may need imaging, sedation or medication, and oral intake has to be cleared by the nurse.

steps.prompt: Continuing your rounds, you reach a 61-year-old man triaged two hours ago for 'indigestion.' He is now gray, sweating through his shirt, and sitting very still.

choices.text: Get the triage or charge nurse immediately, state what changed, and obtain a 12-lead without waiting for the rest of your loop
choices.feedback: Correct. This is why waiting room rounds exist. Gray, diaphoretic, bradycardic and hypotensive with epigastric symptoms is a patient who does not finish your loop in the lobby.

choices.text: Finish rounding on the remaining patients, then report both findings together
choices.feedback: A finding that waits is a finding that was worthless. This one does not keep.

choices.text: Reassure him it is probably his stomach and recheck in 15 minutes
choices.feedback: Interpreting and reassuring is outside scope and, here, dangerously wrong.

choices.text: Walk him back to a room yourself while calling out for the nurse
choices.feedback: Your instinct about acuity is right, but walking a hypotensive, bradycardic patient is unsafe. Get the nurse and a wheelchair or stretcher.

steps.prompt: He is taken straight back and a code STEMI is called from his EKG. Thirty seconds later the man from step one sees this and says, loudly, 'So that's how it works, you have to make a scene.'

choices.text: Acknowledge how it looks, explain without detail that someone's condition changed, do not discuss the other patient, and tell him what you will do next for his wife
choices.feedback: Correct. You cannot explain another patient, ever, but you can name the appearance honestly and redirect to what you control.

choices.text: Explain that the other man was having a heart attack
choices.feedback: A privacy violation in front of a full waiting room. Never disclose another patient's condition, even to defend yourself.

choices.text: Ignore the comment and keep walking
choices.feedback: Silence here reads as confirmation that the system is arbitrary. A brief, honest response costs ten seconds.

choices.text: Tell him that if he continues you will call security
choices.feedback: Wildly disproportionate to a frustrated comment, and it escalates a room full of people who are already on edge.

steps.prompt: Twenty minutes later the charge nurse asks how the lobby is doing.

choices.text: Report by exception: who you rechecked, whose vitals changed, who is vomiting, who has been waiting longest, and the current mood of the room
choices.feedback: Correct. Charge needs exceptions and trends, not a recitation. The mood of the waiting room is operational information too.

choices.text: Say it is fine and everyone is waiting
choices.feedback: You hold information nobody else has. Reporting nothing wastes an entire hour of observation.

choices.text: Report only the complaint from the husband
choices.feedback: The complaint matters, but the clinical reassessments are the part that changes decisions about who comes back next.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: the lobby is a clinical space. Service recovery is listen, acknowledge the specific thing, apologize for the experience, fix what is within reach, and escalate, and none of that involves defending the department or promising a time. Repeat vital signs on waiting patients exist to catch the person who is now worse, and that finding goes to the triage or charge nurse the moment you have it, not at the end of your loop. You can never explain one patient to another, but you can name honestly how something looks and return to what you control.

scenarios.title: Stroke alert: fourteen minutes
scenarios.intro: 1105 on a weekday. EMS calls a stroke alert three minutes out: 72-year-old woman, right-sided weakness and slurred speech, found by her neighbor. You are the tech assigned to the resus side. The stroke team, CT and the pharmacist are being paged now. Department policy targets CT within 25 minutes of arrival.

steps.prompt: The stretcher comes through the bay doors. The neighbor who found her is walking behind the crew, holding her purse and her phone, and looks like she is about to hand them over and leave.

choices.text: Get the last known well time from the neighbor and write down her name and phone number before she leaves, then take the belongings
choices.feedback: Correct. Eligibility for clot-dissolving treatment runs entirely on the last known well time, and the only witness is about to walk out the door.

choices.text: Take the belongings and thank her for coming
choices.feedback: You just lost the most important data point of the call. The purse can wait; the witness cannot.

choices.text: Ask the crew for the onset time instead
choices.feedback: The crew relays what the neighbor told them, which is better than nothing, but the team will need to reach the witness directly and may need to clarify.

choices.text: Direct her to registration to provide the information there
choices.feedback: Registration will not capture a clinical timeline, and she may leave before anyone asks. Get it yourself, now.

steps.prompt: She is on your stretcher. Right arm drift, right facial droop, speech is slurred but she follows commands. The team is gathering. Three tasks are competing: glucose, a measured weight, and vital signs.

choices.text: Glucose first, then the bed-scale weight in kilograms, then the full vital set, calling each out to the recorder
choices.feedback: Correct. Hypoglycemia mimics stroke and is fixable in ninety seconds, and thrombolytic dosing needs a measured weight, not a guess.

choices.text: Vitals first, then glucose, then ask the family for her usual weight
choices.feedback: Vitals matter, but the glucose is the one result that could change the diagnosis outright, and a reported weight is not acceptable for weight-based dosing.

choices.text: Skip the weight since she can tell you what she weighs
choices.feedback: Self-reported and staff-estimated weights are routinely off by enough to matter for a clot-dissolving drug. Use the bed scale.

choices.text: Start with a 12-lead before anything else
choices.feedback: The EKG is on the list but it is not first. Glucose and weight are the two items that change treatment decisions in the next ten minutes.

steps.prompt: Glucose is 112 mg/dL. Weight is 64 kg. CT calls and says the scanner is open now. You have not drawn labs or placed an IV, and the nurse is preparing to do both.

choices.text: Go to CT now; the team can draw labs and place access in the scanner suite or immediately afterward
choices.feedback: Correct. Door-to-CT of about 25 minutes drives everything downstream. Useful tasks done at the wrong moment are the classic error in a stroke alert.

choices.text: Finish labs and two IVs first so nothing is missing for the scan
choices.feedback: This is the trap. Nothing on that list requires being done before imaging, and every minute of delay narrows her options.

choices.text: Ask CT to hold the scanner for five minutes
choices.feedback: Holding the scanner in a stroke alert is backwards. The patient goes to the scanner and the work travels with her.

choices.text: Go now and bring the tubes and IV supplies with you so the nurse can work in the suite
choices.feedback: Good thinking. Moving immediately while carrying the equipment lets both happen without a delay.

steps.prompt: In the scanner suite the patient's daughter arrives, out of breath, and asks you whether her mother had a stroke and whether she will get 'the clot-busting drug.'

choices.text: Say the team is reviewing the scan right now, that the physician will speak with her as soon as they have it, and offer to bring her where she can wait and be found
choices.feedback: Correct. Honest about the process, no interpretation, and it gives a frightened family member something concrete. Then tell the nurse she is here.

choices.text: Tell her the scan looked clear from what you saw on the screen
choices.feedback: Interpreting imaging is outside scope and could be badly wrong. Never do this, even when it seems reassuring.

choices.text: Tell her you cannot discuss anything and walk away
choices.feedback: Accurate about scope but needlessly cold. You can decline to interpret while still being useful and human.

choices.text: Ask her the last known well time and whether her mother takes blood thinners, then relay both to the team
choices.feedback: Excellent. She may have information the neighbor did not, and anticoagulant use directly affects treatment eligibility.

steps.prompt: The scan is done at eighteen minutes from arrival. The team is deciding on treatment and the patient is heading back to the resus bay.

choices.text: Report your timeline to the recorder: arrival time, glucose value and time, measured weight, last known well with the witness's phone number, CT time, and the daughter's added history
choices.feedback: Correct. In an alert, the tech's contribution is the numbers and the times nobody else can reconstruct. Say them out loud so they land in the record.

choices.text: Assume everything you did was already documented by the recorder
choices.feedback: Recorders miss items during a fast alert, particularly the witness contact and the measured weight. Confirm rather than assume.

choices.text: Go clean the bay and catch up on your other rooms
choices.feedback: The bay does need restocking, but not before your times and values are confirmed in the record. Sixty seconds first.

scenarios.debrief: The pattern: a stroke alert is a race against a clock that started before you met the patient. The tech owns the four things nobody else will capture: last known well with a reachable witness, an immediate glucose because hypoglycemia imitates stroke perfectly, a measured weight in kilograms for weight-based dosing, and the timeline itself. Nothing delays the scanner, including labs and IV access, which travel with the patient. And when family arrives, you can be genuinely useful without ever interpreting an image or a result.
